english_translation: Did you hear the folktale about the hare and the baboon that grandmother used to tell us?

dialogue.shona: Wakanzwa nyaya yengano yetsuro negudo yataitaurirwa naambuya here?
dialogue.english: Did you hear the folktale about the hare and the baboon that grandmother used to tell us?
dialogue.literal_gloss: Wakanzwa [you/he (past) nzwa] • nyaya [nyaya] • yengano [yengano] • yetsuro [yetsuro] • negudo [and / with gudo] • yataitaurirwa [yataitaurirwa] • naambuya [naambuya] • here [(yes/no question marker)]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('Wakanzwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Wakanzwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Asking Questions in Shona ('here', 'sei', 'ndeipi')
grammar_notes.content: Forming a yes/no question in Shona is remarkably easy: keep the normal statement word order and simply add the question word 'here' at the very end of the sentence! For example, 'Mvura ichanaya mangwana' ('It will rain tomorrow') becomes 'Mvura ichanaya here mangwana?' ('Will it rain tomorrow?'). For open questions, use 'sei?' ('how / why?', as in 'Wakafamba sei?' = 'How did you travel?') or 'ndeipi?' ('which one?', as in 'Ndeipi mota?' = 'Which car?').
grammar_notes.rule: Statement + here? = Yes/No Question | Verb + sei? = How? | Ndeipi + Noun? = Which [noun]?

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'negudo'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'negudo'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'gudo' forms 'negudo'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

cultural_notes.title: Fireside Folktales ('Ngano') of Tsuro Magen'a (the Clever Hare) & Gudo (the Baboon)
cultural_notes.content: On evenings during the dry harvest season, grandmothers ('ambuya') gathered children by the fire to tell 'ngano' (folktales with call-and-response songs). The most beloved characters are 'Tsuro Magen'a' (the quick-witted hare) and his larger, easily outsmarted uncle 'Gudo' (the baboon).
